passage:
Mahima, sit. You asked why your Deepak Mama went quiet at the sweet shop just now. Let me tell you.
When I was nineteen, my Amma died in the April of my second year. By October I thought I was fine. Marks were back up, I was laughing in the canteen again. Then one morning in the chemistry lecture, someone behind me opened a tiffin of besan laddoos. Amma's Diwali smell, cardamom and roasted gram flour. My eyes just flooded. I had to walk out with the whole class staring.
I sat on the stairs thinking, six months of progress, gone. I was so ashamed.
It took me years to understand I hadn't slipped back at all. Grief moves like the tide, beta. It goes out, it comes in, and the coming in doesn't cancel the going out. Today at the shop was just another wave.

qa.q: What smell set off Deepak's tears in the chemistry lecture?
qa.a: Besan laddoos from a tiffin behind him, Amma's Diwali smell of cardamom and roasted gram flour.

qa.q: What did nineteen-year-old Deepak think and feel as he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: He thought six months of progress were gone and felt ashamed, as if the sudden tears meant he had gone backwards.

qa.q: What could have helped Deepak on those stairs that day?
qa.a: Knowing that grief comes in waves would have let him see the tears as a normal surge rather than a failure, and he could have told a friend what the smell had stirred.

qa.q: How might a classmate in that chemistry lecture have seen Deepak walking out?
qa.a: A classmate might have been confused or worried, seeing only sudden tears and not knowing that the smell of the laddoos had brought back Amma's death.

grounding: Shows a sudden wave of grief triggered by a festival smell in a lecture hall, and the false feeling of having gone backwards.

passage:
The client call was in ten minutes, and Hansa's slides still had a typo on page four. Then the pantry speaker, playing someone's old-songs list, started the harmonium opening of the ghazal her Papa used to hum while shaving.
Seven months, and she had not cried at work once. Now her eyes spilled over before she could stop them. She stood frozen at the whiteboard, marker in hand, thinking, I was doing so well. Why now?
Arohi, from the next desk, glanced over and quietly turned the speaker down. "Want me to open the call while you wash your face?"
Hansa nodded. In the washroom she pressed a wet tissue to her eyes and whispered, "Seven months," as though the number should have protected her.
Four minutes later she walked back in, fixed the typo and unmuted, still not sure what had just happened to her.

qa.q: What was Hansa's Papa's ghazal played on?
qa.a: It came on the pantry speaker, playing someone's old-songs list.

qa.q: What does Hansa's thought 'I was doing so well. Why now?' suggest she believes?
qa.a: She feels shaken and discouraged, as if one sudden wave of tears after seven months undoes all her progress.

qa.q: What could help Hansa once the client call is over?
qa.a: She could remind herself that grief returns in waves, tell Arohi what the song meant, and expect that other reminders like it may come.

qa.q: How might Arohi have read the moment at the whiteboard?
qa.a: Arohi saw a colleague frozen in tears just before a deadline and chose small, practical help, turning the music down and offering to open the call, without asking for explanations.

grounding: Illustrates a song unexpectedly bringing tears at the office months after a death, and the surprise of the wave feeling like a setback.

passage:
Karthik had five minutes before his seminar presentation, the professor already tapping the projector, when someone behind him opened a tiffin. Rasam. Pepper and tamarind, exactly like Amma's.
It had been eight months. He'd been fine for weeks. Fine at Diwali, even.
Now his throat closed and his eyes filled, right there in the second row. He pressed his thumb hard into his palm.
Thomas, beside him, glanced over. "You okay?"
"It's stupid. It's the smell."
"Not stupid." Thomas passed him a tissue without making a show of it. "Want me to go first?"
Karthik nodded. He wasn't going backwards, he told himself. It was just a wave.

qa.q: What was in the tiffin behind Karthik?
qa.a: Rasam.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when his eyes filled in the second row?
qa.a: He felt a sudden wave of grief, surprised and embarrassed, after weeks of feeling fine.

qa.q: What small step helped Karthik get through the moment?
qa.a: Accepting Thomas's quiet tissue and offer to go first, and telling himself it was a wave, not going backwards.

qa.q: What might Thomas be feeling as he passes the tissue?
qa.a: Thomas seems caring and tactful, wanting to help without drawing attention.

grounding: Shows a young man hit by a sudden wave of grief from a familiar smell months later, fearing he is going backwards when he is not.

passage:
The Hyderabad office had strung up Diwali lights over the weekend. Mahima walked in on Monday, saw the rows of little diyas at reception, and had to go straight to the washroom.
Last Diwali, Papa had lit every one of them on their balcony, humming off-key.
She had thought she was doing better. Seven months. She'd laughed at a movie on Saturday. Now she was locked in a cubicle, crying so hard her shoulders shook.
When she came out, Lokesh from her team was at the water cooler. He took one look at her face and said, "Take your time. I'll tell the standup you're running late." Mahima nodded, blew her nose, and went back to the washroom mirror.

qa.q: What did Papa do last Diwali?
qa.a: He lit every diya on their balcony, humming off-key.

qa.q: Why did Mahima feel she had gone backwards?
qa.a: She was shocked and sad, having thought she was doing better, when the lights brought a sudden wave of grief.

qa.q: What could help Mahima see this moment differently?
qa.a: Understanding that grief comes in waves, so a festival reminder is normal, not a sign she is going backwards.

qa.q: How does Lokesh respond to seeing her face?
qa.a: Lokesh seems kind and discreet, giving her time without asking questions and covering for her at the standup.

grounding: Shows a young woman surprised by a wave of grief at festival lights months after her father's death.

passage:
"Reena? Reena, what's wrong?"
"Nothing. It's this song, Noor."
The café speaker was playing an old film melody. Reena's cheeks were wet.
"Your Nana's song?"
"He sang it every morning while shaving. Badly." She laughed and cried at once. "It's been nearly a year. I was fine. Why now?"
"Because you loved him."
"I feel like I'm back at the start."
"You're not. You've had good days. This is just a wave."
"A wave?"
"That's what my aunt calls it. It comes, and then it goes."
Reena wiped her face and held her cup with both hands until the song ended.

qa.q: Who sang the song every morning while shaving?
qa.a: Reena's Nana.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she said "I'm back at the start"?
qa.a: She felt surprised and discouraged, as if the sudden tears meant her grief was undoing itself.

qa.q: How does Noor's word "wave" help Reena?
qa.a: It reminds her grief comes and goes rather than moving in a straight line, so tears don't mean she is going backwards.

qa.q: What might Noor be feeling as she comforts Reena?
qa.a: Noor seems gentle and caring, calm enough to offer her aunt's word for it.

grounding: Shows a young woman caught by a wave of grief when a song plays, fearing she is back at the start, and a friend naming it a wave.

passage: It happened in the middle of a statistics lecture, eight months after Ba died. Someone two rows ahead opened a tiffin, and the smell of methi thepla drifted back. Ba made them every Sunday, burnt on one edge because she never trusted the gas. Before I knew it, tears were dripping onto my notebook. I hadn't cried like that since the thirteenth day. I kept my head down and pretended to write. Zainab, sitting next to me, slid a tissue across without looking and whispered, "Hansa, want to step out?" I shook my head. Afterwards I felt ashamed, as if I had gone backwards, as if I had failed some test of being over it. Zainab said her Dadi's death still came back like that, on random Tuesdays, years later. That helped more than anything.

qa.q: What smell drifted back during the lecture?
qa.a: The smell of methi thepla from someone's tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Hansa feel ashamed after the lecture?
qa.a: Hansa felt ashamed and discouraged, as if crying eight months later meant going backwards.

qa.q: What could help Hansa when the next wave comes?
qa.a: Remembering that grief returns in waves, as Zainab described, and that stepping out for a few minutes is allowed.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab, sitting next to Hansa?
qa.a: Zainab recognises the wave from her own loss, so she quietly offers a tissue and a way out without any fuss.

grounding: Shows a smell bringing sudden tears in a lecture months after a death, and the wave feeling like going backwards when it is not.
